newsitem.title: USA: U.S. drops plans for Zaire security force.
newsitem.headline: U.S. drops plans for Zaire security force.

text.p: The United States has dropped plans to send combat troops to Zaire and instead will send fewer than 1,000 logistical personnel to Rwanda to aid returning refugees, Defence Secretary William Perry said on Tuesday.
Perry said U.S. Air Force and other personnel would go as part of a U.N.-authorised military support operation to be led by Canada and operate chiefly within Rwanda instead of Zaire.

But he stressed that, despite the sudden trek of a half-million refugees back to Rwanda from Zaire in recent days, the situation was fluid and Washington remained ready to send protective troops to Zaire if necessary.

"There have been more than 500,000 refugees that have peacefully returned to Rwanda in the last few days. This is a very positive development and we are modifying our plans based on this dramatic change," Perry told reporters.

"The approach that we are taking is designed to help those that have returned while at the same time leaving the multinational force prepared to help inside Zaire if that were to become necessary," he said.
The U.S. Air Force has already moved teams to airports at Kigali in Rwanda, Mombasa in Kenya, and Entebbe in Uganda, to help move personnel and aid into Rwanda, he added.

"I must emphasise that the situation remains fluid," the U.S. defence secretary said. "For the moment, the peaceful return of so many refugees is a very positive development. But there still remain hundreds of thousands of refugees displaced outside their camps in Zaire. We do not have precise information on their number or location."
A spokesman at Rhein-Main air base in Frankfurt, Germany, told Reuters the first C-17 military cargo aircraft loaded with air traffic control equipment was scheduled to leave for Kigali on Tuesday.

President Bill Clinton last week tentatively authorised the movement of some 1,000 armed troops into Goma, Zaire, to secure the airport there and to establish a corridor to nearby Rwanda for the voluntary return of refugees.
But the sudden flood of refugees home beginning last Friday changed the need for protection and shifted the focus of the Canadian-led effort to Rwanda, Perry said.

"This force will require considerably fewer troops than originally envisioned and will operate chiefly in Rwanda," he said. "Our current thinking is that U.S. contribution to this effort will be less than a thousand troops. And these will be support logistics troops rather than combat troops."

Officials of Canada, the United States and other nations that have pledged to take part in the humanitarian effort will meet at U.S. military headquarters in Stuttgart, Germany, on Thursday to make final plans for the operation, Perry said.

"Meanwhile, between now and then, our small team of less than 100 personnel will remain in Kigali," he said. "It will continue to assess the situation there. It will run a civil-military operation and it will maintain liaison teams.

"These actions allow us to provide assistance to the repatriation effort in Rwanda pending completion of the details of this multinational force. But these actions also provide the basis for a larger mission, should that become necessary."

The State Department on Monday said a U.S. relief team in Rwanda was working with planners in Washington and U.S. diplomats elsewhere to determine how best to help the refugees streaming back to Rwanda.
